# DataQ — session handoff (updated 2026-09-30, end of session)

## Problem statement / context
DataQ is a single-tenant data-quality platform (FastAPI + Celery + GX + React; repo
`TheurgicDuke771/DataQ`, local checkout `~/Coding/Python/DataQ`, conda env `dataq`,
shell is fish/zsh via the Bash tool). It stays a **cloud-hosted product** (Azure/AWS
reference deployments remain the preferred production path). We are retiring only
**our own paid dev/test cloud estate** (AWS, Azure, Snowflake, Databricks) for cost.
After that, development and testing run on the local stack; anything cloud-specific
that can't be run live gets the `needs-cloud-verification` label and is tracked in
**#2224**. **The clouds still exist right now**, so use them while they do: deploy,
live-verify, then plan and execute the teardown (items 1–3 below).

Standing rules (from the user and CLAUDE.md, still in force):
- One functionality per commit. Tests for each change, and **prove a regression
  test fails without its fix**. Run `/code-review --comment low` on every PR (the
  review agent, never a self-review). Fix findings in the same PR, or file an issue.
  Squash-merge.
- **Migrations are additive and ship in their own PR, ahead of the code that uses
  them.** Test up and down locally on a populated scratch DB. For CHECK constraints,
  add them NOT VALID and VALIDATE in an autocommit block. Build indexes CONCURRENTLY.
  Make the migration safe to re-run.
- Never commit a credential. Read secrets inline only; never print them or write
  them to files. Never `cat`/parse `secrets.sh`; only `source` it inline. No
  `--no-verify`.
- **Confirm before any cloud or infra change.** Log every infra change in
  `docs/ops-log.md` with UTC timestamps; write "maintainer's IP", never the address.
  Never touch the harness ADF triggers (`tr_orders_landed`, `tr_customers_daily`,
  both `Stopped`).
- Run the **whole** frontend suite (`pnpm test:coverage`) and the whole backend
  suite (`pytest backend/tests`; no xdist, so no `-n`) before pushing. After any
  backgrounded `git push`, confirm it landed with `git ls-remote --heads origin
  <branch>` against `git rev-parse HEAD`.
- Published docs (`docs/site/`) may not cite ticket numbers; a pre-commit hook
  enforces this.

## What this session shipped
Earlier in the session, all merged:
- Platform-retirement follow-ups #2211–#2250, including JSON flat files, DMF EXPLAIN
  probe, the Athena/Redshift/Azure SQL aggregate lanes, the Ask-AI fix, and
  check-type examples.
- LLM providers live-verified: Azure OpenAI 8/8; Bedrock #2251 fixed in #2252.
- Indirect dependencies: demo compose profile (#2254), masked-through-lineage
  (#2256), pipeline duration/overdue baselines (#2257); CI pip-audit ignore (#2261,
  tracked in #2260).
- **ADR 0047 automated coverage (#1660/#1661):**
  - the ADR (#2258);
  - schema (#2259);
  - reconciler (#2262);
  - `column_profile` metric (#2263);
  - `check_suggestions` table (#2264);
  - **review queue (#2265, merged)**;
  - **automatic suites get a "Column profile is normal" check (#2266, merged)**.

Late in the session, while the clouds were still up (user-approved, all torn down
afterwards, and logged):
- **Column profile live-verified on every SQL engine.** Postgres, MySQL, Databricks,
  Snowflake and Trino were done earlier. Athena, Redshift Serverless and Azure SQL
  were recreated briefly: Athena + Redshift 41 passed, Azure SQL 17 passed.
  - Redshift found **#2267**: one column the engine can't cast to a string
    (GEOMETRY, BOOLEAN) dropped distinct counts for the *whole* table, and SUPER
    objects cast to NULL, so they read 0 distinct.
  - Fixed in **#2268**: a zero-row probe per column finds the uncastable columns, and
    a distinct count is recorded only when the cast kept every value. The payload
    field `distinct_available` became `distinct_unavailable: [columns]`.
  - Re-verified live on all three; review had no findings.
- **ADF pipeline gate (#2230) live-verified** on the harness factory against a
  tunnelled local stack (cloudflared quick tunnel, PAT-only auth; prod predates the
  endpoint). Pass, fail and status-only (`trigger:false`, `created_runs: 0`) all
  behaved correctly.
  - Found **#2269 (security)**: the snippet's `secureOutput`/`secureInput` sat
    outside `policy`, so ADF ignored them and the PAT showed in run history.
  - Fixed in **#2272** with a test pinning the placement; re-verified live (both
    activities now show `**********`).
  - The scratch PAT that was exposed was revoked at once.
- `needs-cloud-verification` removed from #2230, #2263 and #2266; results posted on
  each and on #2224.
- **Main went red** at `7db37ac0`: #2265's new test expected 2 automatic checks, and
  #2266 (merged after it) makes it 3. Filed **#2270**, fixed in **#2271**.
- Ops-log entries for all of the above: **#2273**.

## Open right now (all have auto-merge on)
- **#2271** fixes red main. **Merge it first.** CI was running at close.
- **#2268** (#2267 fix), **#2272** (#2269 fix) and **#2273** (ops log) were
  blocked, because their CI inherited the red-main failure
  (`test_a_profiling_failure_does_not_skip_the_table`).
  → **First action next session:** once #2271 has merged, for each of these three
  branches run `git checkout <branch> && git merge origin/main && git push` (a plain
  push, never force). Confirm CI goes green and auto-merge fires, then check the
  issues closed: `gh issue view 2267 2269 2270`.
  Branches: `fix/issue-2267-column-profile-distinct`,
  `fix/issue-2269-adf-gate-secure-policy`, `chore/ops-log-2266-2230-verification`.
  If a CI job fails, read its log with
  `gh api --allow-escape-sequences repos/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/actions/jobs/<id>/logs`.
- 11 Dependabot PRs (#2180–#2190) haven't been reviewed. #2181 is a SQLAlchemy
  minor bump (2.0 → 2.1) and deserves care.

## Pending action items (in order)
1. **Deploy the latest `main` to both clouds and live-verify every feature.**
   Do this once the four PRs above have merged.
   - Deployed today: Azure `517b407b` (2026-09-28; 81 commits and **6 migrations**
     behind); AWS `aws-7a3244a4` (2026-09-07; 177 commits and **16 migrations**
     behind).
   - Follow `deploy/README.md`:
     - pre-deploy checklist;
     - `tofu plan` then apply on `deploy/terraform/azure` and
       `deploy/terraform/aws`, reviewing drift before applying;
     - the `deploy.yml` / `deploy-aws.yml` `workflow_dispatch` runs; migrate must
       exit 0;
     - verify the image SHA on api, worker, frontend **and beat** separately;
     - `alembic_version` read back on both databases;
     - required post-deploy scripts (for example
       `backend/scripts/redact_stale_incident_evidence.py`).
   - Then the full post-deploy smoke **plus an authenticated WRITE probe** on each
     cloud, and a feature-by-feature live walkthrough. The #2224 checklist is the
     list to work through:
     - sign-in and sign-out (Entra ID, Cognito, OTP), PATs over `/mcp/`;
     - every datasource type's connection test and a suite run;
     - monitors: freshness, volume, schema drift, anomaly incl. `column_profile`,
       aggregate, comparison;
     - automatic coverage: turn on `auto_coverage` on one connection, watch the
       reconciler create a suite, check the review queue's accept/reject;
     - the pipeline gate from ADF against the **deployed** app;
     - alerts (Teams/Slack/email/SES), assets/lineage/incidents, the MCP tools,
       LLM features, DMF, DQX, the security headers, CSP and WAF.
   - Record the results in `docs/ops-log.md`. File any defect found (fixed or
     filed), and remove `needs-cloud-verification` from each item verified.
   - Confirm with the user before `tofu apply` and before each deploy.
2. **Write a detailed teardown plan for all four: AWS, Azure, Snowflake and
   Databricks.** Present it to the user for approval; execute nothing yet.
   - Per platform: a full inventory, read live rather than from memory:
     - resource groups and resources;
     - ECS/RDS/ElastiCache/CloudFront/WAF/Cognito/Secrets Manager/SSM/ECR/S3/IAM
       users, roles and GitHub OIDC;
     - Container Apps, Postgres, Key Vault, ADF, AI Services, storage, Entra app
       registrations;
     - Snowflake warehouses, databases, roles, users, PATs and tags;
     - Databricks workspace, SQL warehouse, catalogs and tokens.
   - For each resource: its dependencies, the ordered deletion steps, a way to
     verify it's gone, and its cost impact.
   - **Backups first**: prod Postgres dumps, any data worth keeping, the
     `docs/ops-log.md` identifiers, and exported Terraform state.
   - **Credential retirement**: every KV / Secrets Manager secret, PATs, GitHub
     secrets and variables, the `production` environment.
   - What must **stay**: the published Terraform in `deploy/terraform/*` (#1384 and
     #1385 stay open for it), GHCR images, docs.
   - What breaks locally once each platform is gone: the harness, and #2224's
     re-verification list.
   - The Databricks token lapse (#2145), and the #588 (Snowflake harness leg) and
     #590 (Azure estate) decision gates.
   - Rollback / "recreate from IaC" notes.
3. **Execute the teardown** only after the user approves the plan, step by step with
   confirmation and an ops-log entry per step. Then epic **#2220** (two local
   paths):
   - keep the authless contributor stack as it is, hidden from user docs;
   - make the OTP stack in `docker-compose.ghcr.yml` the production-like default,
     with HTTPS via a local CA auto-installed into the OS trust store, rate
     limiting, sole ingress and TLS everywhere.
4. **ADR 0047 phase 3c:** queue the LLM check suggester's output with
   `source='llm'` (`llm_checksuggest.py` → `suggestion_service.propose`).
5. **ADR 0047 phase 4:**
   - a coverage % figure (share of inventory assets watched by at least one suite
     that ran in the last 7 days, automatic-only vs authored) and a false-positive
     rate (incidents resolved `false_positive` among automatic-suite incidents), both
     on the dashboard;
   - a `resolution` choice in the incident resolve API and UI;
   - MCP read tools for coverage and the queue (keep the MCP honesty rules; derive
     the tool counts from `tests/support/mcp_gates.GATES`).
6. **Docs examples**, the rest of the earlier request:
   - Tier 1 item 2: one example connection config and target per datasource in
     `docs/site/guides/datasources-checks.md`;
   - Tier 1 item 3: a REST API curl walkthrough against the local stack;
   - Tier 2: API/CLI snippets in the guides, config and a sample result per monitor
     kind;
   - Tier 3: MCP tool examples and a troubleshooting page.
7. Follow-ups: #2253 (demo-profile walkthrough on the marketing page), #2255 (a
   masking reason per `redacted_columns` entry; security-sensitive), #2260 (oauthlib
   4), #2224 (whatever item 1 doesn't cover).
8. Refresh the `docs/progress.md` snapshot (open PR/issue counts), and CLAUDE.md
   §13 once the deploy and teardown change the headline.
9. Housekeeping, ask before removing any of it:
   - about 50 old `dataq_test_*`/`dataq_mig_*`/`dataq_perf*` scratch databases in
     `dataq-postgres-1`;
   - the `perf/issue-1645-one-connection` worktree;
   - stopped harness containers;
   - `cloudflared`, installed via Homebrew this session (`brew uninstall
     cloudflared`).

## Useful local facts
- The local dev stack (compose project `dataq`: postgres, redis, openbao, mailpit)
  holds a prod-mirror dataset. Never disturb it; use scratch DBs and a spare Redis
  db index for live tests.
- A scratch API + worker with PAT-only auth (safe to expose through a tunnel): OTP
  mode with a dummy mailer. Set `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS=false` and `AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_HOST`,
  `AUTH_EMAIL_USERNAME`, `AUTH_EMAIL_FROM`, `AUTH_EMAIL_PASSWORD_SECRET_NAME`,
  `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS`. Mint the PAT with `api_key_service.create_key`.
- Cloud live-lane recipes (Athena IAM user + Glue DB, Redshift Serverless
  `dataq-it-rs`, Azure SQL free-offer DB, seeded with `mssql_tds.install()`) are in
  the 2026-09-28/29 ops-log entries. The lane env names are `ATHENA_TEST_*`,
  `REDSHIFT_TEST_*` (the admin secret is `redshift!dataq-it-rs-dqadmin`) and
  `DATAQ_MSSQL_LIVE_*`.
- The ADF gate snippet's run history on `dataq-harness-adf` from 2026-09-29 22:38Z
  holds a revoked scratch PAT. It is dead, and the history can't be deleted.
- The working tree is on `chore/ops-log-2266-2230-verification`. Check out `main`
  and pull before starting.

== 1977
## Problem / motivation

DataQ has no first-class concept of a **data contract** — a versioned, shared spec of a table's schema + quality rules + SLA that both the team producing a dataset and the teams consuming it can validate against. Today a consumer can author ad hoc checks against a landed table, but there's no way to say "these checks exist *because* they enforce contract v3" or to trace a failure back to the specific contract clause it broke.

This issue scopes the **consumer-side half only** — validating data already at rest against a contract, using DataQ's existing GX-based check/suite execution. It's deliberately split from producer-side (pre-publish, data-in-motion) validation, which would need a separate lightweight enforcement library embedded in a producer's own pipeline — see "Out of scope" below.

## Proposed change

1. **`contracts` table** — `id`, `name`, `version`, `domain`/`owner`, `status` (draft/active/deprecated), `spec` (JSONB holding the contract document), timestamps.
2. **Suite linkage** — an optional `contract_id` + `contract_version` on `suite`, so a suite can be tagged as enforcing a specific contract without changing today's suite model (a suite with no contract works exactly as it does now).
3. **[Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)](https://bitol-io.github.io/open-data-contract-standard/) import** — parse an ODCS YAML document into a `contracts` row, then auto-generate the corresponding checks in a linked suite: schema fields → `expectation`/`schema_drift` checks, quality rules → `expectation` checks, `slaProperties` → freshness/volume monitor-kinds. Reuses the existing `import_suite` machinery with an ODCS→DataQ-suite translation step in front of it.
4. **ODCS export** — serialize a contract (+ current suite/check state) back to ODCS YAML, mirroring `export_suite`'s shape. This is the document a future producer-side validator would consume, so both sides stay provably aligned.
5. **Traceability on violations** — when a contract-linked suite's check (particularly `schema_drift`) fails, tag the resulting incident with `contract_id` + the specific violated field/rule, so triage starts at "which clause of the contract broke" instead of a bare check name.
6. **Read surface** — REST + MCP read tools: `get_contract`, `list_contracts`, and a compliance rollup (pass/fail across a contract's linked suite(s)), following the existing asset/incident read-tool pattern (ADR 0008 Tier 1 style — read-only, no new write-gated capability needed beyond normal suite/check permissions).

=== 2032
Found by `/code-review` on #2031 (the pyiceberg 0.11.1 → 0.12.0 bump). The bump does not *cause* this, but it makes an existing inefficiency both louder and measurable.

## What

`load_iceberg_table` (`backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py`) calls `pyiceberg.catalog.load_catalog(...)` on **every** call, and it is called once per table load — the check runner, the column profiler, schema drift and the dataset reader each build their own. Nothing caches the catalog handle for the lifetime of a run.

Under 0.11.1 that was merely wasteful. 0.12.0 adds two things that make it visible:

1. **`SqlCatalog.__init__` now always issues probe `SELECT`s** (`SELECT 1 FROM iceberg_tables`, `SELECT iceberg_type FROM iceberg_tables LIMIT 0`). In 0.11.1, `init_catalog_tables=false` meant construction did zero DB round-trips; in 0.12.0 the probe runs regardless.
2. **A catalog DB created before 0.12.0 logs a WARNING on every construction**: `SqlCatalog detected a v0 schema (iceberg_type column missing). The catalog will operate in v0 mode. To migrate, set schema_version='v1'.`

So a 20-check Iceberg suite on a `catalog_type: sql` connection emits roughly 20 identical WARNING lines and 20 catalog handshakes per run, on the same log stream used for run triage. Verified live: the warning was observed reading a table whose catalog DB had been written by 0.11.1.

## Why it matters

- **Log noise on the triage stream.** Repeated identical WARNINGs about a benign, permanent condition train a reader to skim past warnings on the one surface where a real one needs to be seen.
- **Wasted round-trips** against the catalog DB, scaling with check count rather than with connections.

## Not the fix

Setting `schema_version='v1'` silences the warning but issues an `ALTER TABLE iceberg_tables ADD COLUMN iceberg_type VARCHAR(5)` — a DDL write from what is otherwise a read-only consumer, against a catalog DataQ does not own. We should not be migrating a customer's catalog schema as a side effect of running a check.

## Suggested shape

Cache the catalog handle per `(connection, resolved properties)` for the duration of a run, so the handshake and the warning happen once rather than once per table load. The credential is already resolved per load, so the cache key has to include whatever the secret resolves to, and the entry must not outlive a credential rotation.

## Acceptance

- A multi-check Iceberg suite run on a `catalog_type: sql` connection performs **one** catalog construction, not one per check.
- The v0 WARNING appears at most once per run.
- No DDL is issued against the customer's catalog.
- Credential rotation is still picked up (a cached handle must not serve a stale credential).

=== 2018
Split out of the #1328 review so the trade-off is on record rather than only in a code comment.

`dataset_reader._iceberg_read` used to preflight with `scan().count()` (the exact live row count). #1328 moved it to `planned_row_count` — the sum of the manifests' `record_count` — because pyiceberg's `count()` materialises any merge-on-read task **in full, with the whole projection**, to count it: the preflight that exists to avoid a large read was performing one.

Planning cannot read data on any table shape, and it is the better memory predictor (row-level deletes are applied *after* the files are read, so a deleted row still costs its memory). But it is an **upper bound on the live count**, so an Iceberg comparison side with many unmerged deletes — say 150k rows in the data files of which 60k are deleted, against `COMPARISON_MAX_ROWS=100000` — is now refused although its live count is 90k.

Why this is probably right as shipped:

- `COMPARISON_MAX_ROWS` is documented (ADR 0015) as a **memory** guardrail, not a semantic limit, and the planned count is what the worker actually holds.
- The post-read `len(df) > max_rows` check still catches the exact case, so nothing is silently truncated either way.
- The refusal is loud and names the number.

What would make it wrong: a workload on a heavily merge-on-read table where the refusal is a false positive often enough to matter. If that shows up, the fix is to fall back to the exact count **only** when the planned count exceeds the cap *and* the snapshot summary proves there are no row-level deletes (`_row_delete_guard`), so the expensive path is never the one taken on a delete-bearing table.

Not urgent: no consumer is known to compare an Iceberg side near the cap. Filing it so the decision is recorded rather than re-derived.
--- comment: ### pyiceberg 0.12.0 still cannot write delete files — this stays blocked

Checked while taking the 0.11.1 → 0.12.0 bump in #2031, since the blocker for the adversarial merge-on-read test here is `pyiceberg`'s inability to *produce* one locally.

**Answer: still no.** `Table.delete()` in 0.12.0 carries the identical line it had in 0.11.1:

```python
warnings.warn("Merge on read is not yet supported, falling back to copy-on-write", stacklevel=2)
```

- `delete()`, `overwrite()` and `upsert()` are all copy-on-write — they rewrite or drop whole Parquet data files and emit DELETE/OVERWRITE snapshots. No positional deletes, no deletion vectors, no equality deletes are ever written.
- Setting `write.delete.mode=merge-on-read` on the table still only produces that warning and falls back.
- Equality deletes remain unreadable as well (`NotImplementedError`).

What 0.12.0 *did* add is all **read**-side: deletion-vector extraction from Puffin ([#3491](https://github.com/apache/iceberg-python/pull/3491)), zstd Puffin blob decompression ([#3575](https://github.com/apache/iceberg-python/pull/3575)) and a DV spec framing fix ([#3576](https://github.com/apache/iceberg-python/pull/3576)). Useful if the table comes from Spark — useless for building the fixture.

So the constraint recorded in `test_the_probe_never_counts_through_the_driver` is unchanged; #2031 only re-pins its docstring from "0.11.1" to "0.12.0" so the version reference doesn't rot. Building the adversarial table still needs a non-pyiceberg writer (Spark or iceberg-rust) to produce the delete files.

Worth re-checking on the next minor.

def scan_row_count(table: Any) -> int:
    """LIVE rows in the table's current snapshot — exact, and not always cheap.

    ``DataScan.count()`` sums per-file record counts from metadata only while a
    task's filter is fully satisfied and it carries no delete files; a
    merge-on-read task is instead materialised in full to be counted. Callers
    that are guarding a materialisation want `planned_row_count`, which cannot
    read data.

    ``int()`` because the value crosses a driver boundary.
    """
    return int(table.scan().count())

        total += _VARIABLE_CELL_BYTES + int(_VARIABLE_BYTES_FACTOR * mean)

def planned_row_count(table: Any) -> int:
    """Rows the scan will READ from data files — manifest metadata, never a data read.

    An upper bound on the live count, and the right number for a memory guard:
    row-level deletes are applied *after* the files are read, so a deleted row
    still costs its memory. A snapshot-less table plans no files and answers 0.
    """
    return sum(int(task.file.record_count) for task in table.scan().plan_files())


def enforce_iceberg_row_cap(table: Any, *, target: str) -> None:
    """Probe the snapshot from metadata and refuse an over-cap materialisation (#1328).

    Skipped entirely when the cap is disabled — an operator who turns it off does
    not keep paying for a probe nobody reads.

    cap = get_settings().iceberg_scan_row_cap
    if cap <= 0:
        return
    enforce_row_cap(
        planned_row_count(table),
        cap=cap,
        target=f"the current snapshot of table {target!r}",
        remedy=ICEBERG_ROW_CAP_REMEDY,

def _row_delete_guard(summary: Any) -> str | None:
    """``None`` when the summary PROVES the snapshot has zero row-level deletes; otherwise the
    degrade reason.

    for key in _DELETE_TOTAL_KEYS:
        raw = _summary_get(summary, key)
        if raw is None:
            return f"snapshot summary omits {key} — cannot prove no row-level deletes"
        count = _summary_int(summary, key)
        if count is None:
            return f"unparseable snapshot summary field {key}"
        if count > 0:
            return f"row-level deletes present ({key}={count})"
    return None

    """Why a volume/freshness monitor would have to scan rather than answer from snapshot
    metadata, or ``None`` when the metadata answers (or there is no snapshot to read).

    Freshness can additionally fall back per file (missing bounds, attached delete files); that
    is only visible by planning the scan and reads a single column.
    """
    snapshot = table.current_snapshot()
    if snapshot is None:
        return None
    summary = getattr(snapshot, "summary", None)
    if _summary_int(summary, "total-records") is None:
        return "snapshot summary lacks total-records"

    """``(total_records, delta_detail)`` from the current snapshot's summary (#859)."""
    snapshot = table.current_snapshot()
    if snapshot is None:
        return None, {"fallback_reason": "table has no current snapshot"}
    summary = getattr(snapshot, "summary", None)
    total = _summary_int(summary, "total-records")
    if total is None:
        return None, {"fallback_reason": "snapshot summary lacks total-records"}
    guard = _row_delete_guard(summary)
    if guard is not None:
        return None, {"fallback_reason": guard}
    delta: dict[str, Any] = {}
    added = _summary_int(summary, "added-records")
    deleted = _summary_int(summary, "deleted-records")
    if added is not None:
        delta["added_records"] = added
    if deleted is not None:
        delta["deleted_records"] = deleted
    return total, delta

    from pyiceberg.conversions import from_bytes

# Catalog backends pyiceberg's ``load_catalog`` understands.
IcebergCatalogType = Literal["rest", "sql", "glue", "hive"]

# Catalog types whose connection needs a URI (REST endpoint, SQL/metastore URI).
_URI_REQUIRED: frozenset[str] = frozenset({"rest", "sql", "hive"})

# The pyiceberg ADLS FileIO property family whose value is a SAS — and therefore the only
# ``secret_property`` whose credential states its own expiry (#838).
_SAS_PROPERTY_PREFIX = "adls.sas-token"

# `properties` KEYS pyiceberg documents as holding a credential directly (not a reference to one) —
# a literal value here is exactly the #754/#826 leak.
_CREDENTIAL_PROPERTY_KEYS: frozenset[str] = frozenset({"s3.secret-access-key", "adls.account-key"})
# Generic name-based hints — anything that reads as a password/token by NAME, not just the two known
# keys above (a future catalog/storage backend's property family is unknowable in advance).
_CREDENTIAL_NAME_HINTS: tuple[str, ...] = ("password", "token")
_CREDENTIAL_NAME_EXEMPTIONS: frozenset[str] = frozenset({"s3.access-key-id"})


def _looks_like_a_credential_property(key: str) -> bool:
    """True when `key` names something pyiceberg treats as (or that reads like)
    a literal credential, rather than a non-secret identifier or option.
    """
    lowered = key.lower()
    if lowered in _CREDENTIAL_NAME_EXEMPTIONS:
        return False
    if lowered in _CREDENTIAL_PROPERTY_KEYS or lowered.startswith(_SAS_PROPERTY_PREFIX):
        return True
    return any(hint in lowered for hint in _CREDENTIAL_NAME_HINTS)


class IcebergConfig(BaseModel):
    """Non-secret Iceberg catalog + storage config (the credential is the secret)."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")

    catalog_name: str = "default"
    catalog_type: IcebergCatalogType
    catalog_uri: str | None = None
    warehouse: str | None = None
    properties: dict[str, str] = {}
    secret_property: str | None = None
    # A SecretStore *key name*, not a credential — safe to keep in non-secret config
    # (same idiom as the `*_WEBHOOK_SECRET_NAME` settings).
    catalog_secret_name: str | None = None

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def _uri_present(self) -> IcebergConfig:
        if self.catalog_type in _URI_REQUIRED and not self.catalog_uri:
            raise ValueError(f"catalog_uri is required for a {self.catalog_type!r} catalog")
        return self

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def _uri_carries_no_password(self) -> IcebergConfig:
        """Reject a password smuggled into `catalog_uri` (#754 AC2)."""
        if self.catalog_uri and uri_password(self.catalog_uri):
            raise ValueError(
                "catalog_uri must not embed a password (config is stored and returned "
                "in plaintext, and becomes the asset's lineage identity). Put the "
                "catalog credential in the secret store and name it via "
                "'catalog_secret_name'; keep the username in the URI."
            )
        return self

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def _properties_carry_no_credential(self) -> IcebergConfig:
        """Reject a credential smuggled into `properties` (#754/#826, extended to
        the properties dict by #1181's editor exposure).
        """
        for key, value in self.properties.items():
            if _looks_like_a_credential_property(key):
                raise ValueError(
                    f"properties[{key!r}] looks like a credential-bearing property and "
                    "must not carry a literal value (config is stored and returned in "
                    "plaintext). Use 'secret_property' for the storage credential or "
                    "'catalog_secret_name' for the catalog password instead."
                )
            if uri_password(value):
                raise ValueError(
                    f"properties[{key!r}] must not embed a password in a URI-shaped "
                    "value (config is stored and returned in plaintext). Put the "
                    "credential in the secret store instead."
                )
        return self

    def catalog_properties(
        self, secret: str | None, catalog_secret: str | None = None
    ) -> dict[str, str]:
        """The keyword properties handed to ``pyiceberg.catalog.load_catalog``."""
        props: dict[str, str] = dict(self.properties)
        props["type"] = self.catalog_type
        if self.catalog_uri:
            # The catalog credential is re-attached HERE and nowhere else — the last possible
            # moment, in memory, for this one load.
            props["uri"] = (
                inject_uri_password(self.catalog_uri, catalog_secret)
                if catalog_secret
                else self.catalog_uri
            )
        if self.warehouse:
            props["warehouse"] = self.warehouse
        if self.secret_property and secret is not None:
            props[self.secret_property] = secret
        return props

    # authenticates against), `secret_property` (which property it fills, so repointing it hands

    # a UI key-value editor since #1181, where `s3.endpoint` or `adls.account-name` redirect
    # storage just as effectively.
    destination_fields: ClassVar[dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]] = {
        "catalog": ("catalog_uri",),
        "secret": ("catalog_uri", "warehouse", "properties", "secret_property"),
    }

    # A credential-less catalog (local warehouse, vended-credentials REST) is a legitimate config
    # (ADR 0030 §3, the class docstring above).
    secret_optional = True

    def validate_config(self, raw: dict[str, Any]) -> IcebergConfig:
        return IcebergConfig.model_validate(raw)

    def credential_expiry(self, raw: dict[str, Any], secret: str, **_: Any) -> datetime | None:
        """When the storage credential stops working (#838), or ``None``."""
        if not (self.validate_config(raw).secret_property or "").startswith(_SAS_PROPERTY_PREFIX):

        return azure_sas_expiry(secret)

    def test(
        self,
        raw: dict[str, Any],
        secret: str | None,
        *,
        catalog_secret: str | None = None,
        **_: Any,
    ) -> None:
        """Load the catalog, list namespaces, and load the first table found; raise on failure.

        Listing touches only the catalog, so a wrong or unauthorised STORAGE credential tested
        green and failed every read (#1274). Loading one table reads its metadata file from the
        warehouse with that credential. A catalog with no table can only be checked this far.

        from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog

        config = self.validate_config(raw)
        catalog: Any = load_catalog(
            config.catalog_name, **config.catalog_properties(secret, catalog_secret)
        )
        for namespace in catalog.list_namespaces()[:_TEST_NAMESPACE_SCAN]:
            tables = catalog.list_tables(namespace)
            if tables:
                catalog.load_table(tables[0])
                return

@celery_app.task(  # type: ignore[untyped-decorator]  # celery task decorator is unannotated
    name="run_suite", bind=True, max_retries=None
)
def run_suite(
    self: Any,
    run_id: str,
    admission: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    admission_deadline: float | None = None,
) -> str:
    """Worker entry point. ``run_id`` is a string so it serialises over JSON.

    ``admission``/``admission_deadline`` are carried across the task's own re-queues (#1998)
    so a run waiting for worker memory neither re-probes the store nor waits without end;
    a first dispatch never sets them.
    """
    rid = uuid.UUID(run_id)
    session = get_session()
    try:
        decision = _admit_run(
            self, session, run_id=rid, admission=admission, deadline=admission_deadline
        )
        if decision is not None:
            return decision
        # OpenLineage START/terminal brackets the run (ADR 0034, #758) — fail-open, dark by default.
        lineage_dispatch.emit_run_lineage_start(session, run_id=rid)
        try:
            outcome = _run_suite(session, run_id=rid)
        except BaseException:
            lineage_dispatch.emit_run_lineage_terminal(session, run_id=rid)
            raise
        lineage_dispatch.emit_run_lineage_terminal(session, run_id=rid)
        # Incident rollup BEFORE alert dispatch so the report can reference the
        # open incident (#761); fail-soft like the hooks around it.
        incident_service.sync_incidents_for_run(session, run_id=rid)
        alert_dispatch.publish_run_outcome(session, run_id=rid)
        _alert_datasource_health_for_run(session, run_id=rid)
        return outcome
    finally:
        run_admission.release(rid)
        session.close()


def _admit_run(
    task: Any,
    session: Session,
    *,
    run_id: uuid.UUID,
    admission: dict[str, Any] | None,
    deadline: float | None,
) -> str | None:
    """Reserve worker memory for the run, or re-queue it. Returns a terminal outcome string
    when the caller must stop (only a cancel), otherwise ``None`` to proceed.

    Memory pressure never fails a run: it defers, and past the wait budget it proceeds anyway
    rather than starving — logged, and visible on the run as `awaiting_worker_memory` in the
    meantime so "waiting for the worker" is never rendered as "running".
    """
    run = session.get(Run, run_id)
    if run is None:
        return None  # `_run_suite` logs and classifies the missing run
    if run.status == "cancelled":
        # A cancel during a wait must end the wait, not keep re-queueing forever.
        run_admission.set_queued_reason(session, run=run, reason=None)
        log.info("run_suite_already_cancelled", run_id=str(run_id))
        return "cancelled"

    estimate = (
        run_admission.from_carry(admission)
        if admission
        else run_admission.estimate_run_memory(session, run)
    )
    settings = get_settings()
    # Wall clock, deliberately: the deadline is serialised into the retry and read back in a
    # DIFFERENT process, where a monotonic epoch means nothing.
    now = time.time()
    deadline = deadline if deadline is not None else now + settings.run_admission_max_wait_seconds
    outcome = run_admission.admit(session, run=run, estimate=estimate, waited_out=now >= deadline)
    if outcome.defer:
        run_admission.set_queued_reason(session, run=run, reason=run_admission.AWAITING_MEMORY)
        raise task.retry(
            countdown=settings.run_admission_retry_seconds,
            # `args=()` is load-bearing: `signature_from_request` keeps the ORIGINAL
            # positional args when only `kwargs` is passed, and `dispatch_run` publishes
            # `run_id` positionally — so the retry would bind it twice and die with a
            # TypeError instead of re-queueing.
            args=(),
            kwargs={
                "run_id": str(run_id),
                "admission": run_admission.carry(estimate),
                "admission_deadline": deadline,
            },
        )
    run_admission.set_queued_reason(session, run=run, reason=None)
    return None

class RunOnlySession:

    def __init__(self, run: Run | None) -> None:

        return self.run if model is Run else None

## Summary
- Every Iceberg table load built its own pyiceberg catalog: admission probe, check run, monitors, schema drift and profiling each built one. A multi-check run did one catalog handshake per load. On a SQL catalog written before pyiceberg 0.12, each of those handshakes logged the same v0-schema WARNING on the run-triage stream.
- `run_suite` now opens `iceberg_catalog_scope()`. Inside it, `load_iceberg_catalog` reuses one handle per connection. The cache key is a hash of the **resolved** catalog properties, so a rotated credential builds a new handle rather than being served a stale one. On exit, each SQL catalog's SQLAlchemy engine is disposed; a failing dispose is logged and never escapes.
- Outside a scope (API-side Test Connection, profiling, column listing), behaviour is unchanged: nothing is cached. No DDL is ever issued against the customer's catalog; `schema_version='v1'` is deliberately not used.

## Linked issue
Fixes #2032

- [x] fix — bug fix (linked issue above)

- [x] **`docs/progress.md` — N/A** for this PR (Week 6 is closed out with the milestone)
- [x] **Security implications considered**: the cache holds the same resolved properties the catalog object already held, is keyed on a sha256 digest rather than plaintext, and lives only for one task invocation.

## Schema migration?
- [x] No schema change

## Manual test notes
- New tests use a **real** pyiceberg `SqlCatalog` (sqlite + local warehouse). They cover:
  - one construction for five loads inside a scope;
  - one construction per load outside a scope;
  - a rotated token builds a second handle;
  - the engine is disposed at exit;
  - a failing dispose is swallowed.
- A task-level test proves `run_suite` shares one handle between the admission probe and the run body.
- **Mutation-checked:**
  - Bypassing the cache fails 4 tests.
  - Replacing the task's scope with `nullcontext()` fails the task-level test.
- Full backend suite: 8122 passed, 97.10% coverage.

## Security / risk notes
The cache is per-task and never shared across runs. A worker process that runs many suites therefore doesn't accumulate handles or stale credentials.

Result:
I found no bugs in PR #2285 ("one catalog handle per connection for a whole run"), so nothing was posted as a PR comment.

What I checked in `backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py` and `backend/app/worker/tasks.py`:
- **Coverage of the run:** the new scope wraps the admission step as well, so the table load in `run_admission.py` reuses the same catalog handle as the checks.
- **Cache key:** the catalog properties are all strings, so building the key can't fail. The key is hashed, so the secret is never stored in plain text, and a rotated credential produces a new key and a new handle.
- **Threads:** nothing on the run path uses threads, so the per-context cache can't be shared or lost between threads.
- **Early exits:** when the run is re-queued or refused at admission, or raises an error, the scope still closes. Its cleanup happens before the admission slot is released and the database session is closed, which is the right order.
- **Cleanup:** closing the SQL catalog's database connections is new; before, they were simply abandoned. A REST catalog's HTTP session is still never closed, but that was already true when a catalog was built for every table load, so this PR doesn't make it worse.
- **Freshness:** reloading a table on a cached catalog still fetches its metadata again, so a run never reads stale snapshots.

That is the right number for a memory guard: row-level deletes are applied after the files are read, so a deleted row still costs its memory. But it is an upper bound on the live count, and the refusal stated it as the table's size ("has 150000 rows") when the live count may be under the cap.
- When the snapshot summary can't prove zero row-level deletes, the refusal now:
  - says the count is **read from data files**;
  - names the reason (for example `row-level deletes present (total-position-deletes=6)`);
  - points at compaction;
  - carries `count: "planned"` and `row_deletes` in `detail`.

  A delete-free snapshot keeps the exact wording, because its planned count is its live count. If the snapshot metadata can't be read, the refusal still goes out with the plain wording, and `row_deletes` records that the metadata was unreadable.
- **Why not the fallback the issue suggested:** "use the exact count when the planned count is over the cap *and* the summary proves no deletes" can never change an outcome. Without deletes, every data file's `record_count` is exact, so planned == live, and the only false positives are exactly the delete-bearing tables that fallback excludes. The Iceberg spec's `total-records` summary field doesn't subtract deletes either, so there is no metadata-only live count. What was actually wrong was the message, and that is what this PR fixes.

import re
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

)

def test_a_published_tool_count_matches_the_server(page: str) -> None:

    assert counts, f"{page} no longer states a tool count; drop it from _PAGES"
    assert set(counts) == {len(GATES)}

### Workspace membership: the next deploy must go through the workflow

The `workspace_members` migration and the code that reads it are on `main` in
separate steps and neither has rolled yet. The Deploy workflow runs
`alembic upgrade head` **before** it rolls images, so a normal deploy is safe in
either order. A hand-rolled image roll — `az containerapp update`, or a revision
rollback — ahead of the migration is not: the app would find no table.

The app degrades rather than failing (a missing table reads as "membership is not
enforced", with a `membership_table_missing` WARNING per process), so the
symptom is a log line, not an outage. Roll through the workflow anyway; the
fail-safe is a floor, not a plan.

## Pre-deploy checklist

Confirm the change is *ready and green* before you push it to prod:

- [ ] **Everything intended is merged to `main`** and you're deploying that known SHA (blank
  `image_tag` → the immutable commit SHA).
- [ ] **CI is fully green** on that SHA — lint, format, type-check, **all unit + integration
  tests**, the security scans (Bandit / CodeQL / secret-scan / dependency-audit), and the
  frontend E2E. The local verification battery (the same gate) passes too — don't let CI be
  the first feedback loop.
- [ ] **Docs are up to date** for what's shipping — `CLAUDE.md` §13 headline + `docs/progress.md`
  ticked; an **ADR** for any significant decision; the **env-var reference** + this deploy
  guide for any new config; and **user docs** for any new user-facing feature.
- [ ] **DB migrations are safe** — additive/backward-compatible (nullable `ADD COLUMN` / new
  table; no `DROP`/rename/`NOT NULL`-without-default in the same PR as the code that needs
  it), `upgrade` **and** `downgrade` tested locally. The workflow runs `alembic upgrade head`
  **before** rolling the apps, so old code never sees a missing column — you just confirm the
  revision is safe. *Note:* an `ALTER` on a hot table (`runs` / `results` / `pipeline_runs`)
  can block on a live-worker lock and hang the migrate job (#605); recovery + root-cause
  hardening are in [#708](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/708).
- [ ] **Migration-specific pre-deploy steps have been run.** Some revisions need a manual step
  against the live database *before* the migrate job runs, and that step lives in the
  **migration's own docstring** — not here, because it is revision-specific and would rot if
  duplicated. Before deploying, list the revisions that are pending on prod
  (`alembic current` vs `alembic heads`) and read each one's docstring in
  `backend/alembic/versions/` for a **`MANDATORY PRE-DEPLOY`** section; run what it says and
  confirm the result is clean. First instance: **`7d25617cfaf0`** (users nullable
  `aad_object_id` + unique `lower(email)`, #735) requires a duplicate-email audit — if it
  finds duplicates, the index creation fails and the migrate job aborts, so resolve them
  first.
- [ ] **Config + secrets are in place** — the required GitHub env/vars and Key Vault secrets
  (see the [prerequisites](#before-you-deploy-production-prerequisites) above), especially any
  new key this release reads.

### Post-deploy smoke checklist

After the workflow is green, confirm the app is actually **healthy and fully functional** —
don't stop at HTTP 200s. Work top-down:

- [ ] **It's up & reachable** — `GET /healthz` → 200; the SPA root and a deep link load.
- [ ] **A user can sign in** — complete the Azure AD SSO flow end-to-end and land on the
  dashboard as a real user (not just the login screen).
- [ ] **The UI renders correctly** — walk the key pages (Dashboard, Connections, Suites,
  Results, Profile, Admin) and confirm they render with data and **no console / network
  errors**, on **desktop *and* mobile** viewports. (The `ui-tester` agent automates this.)
- [ ] **Every high-level capability works end-to-end** — spot-check the core flows, e.g.:
  add/edit a connection and **test** it; author a check; **trigger a run** and see live
  progress → results → (redacted) failing samples; view dashboard trends; a schedule; an

## AWS deployment

DataQ runs as a **fully independent, live deployment on AWS** (since 2026-08-15) —
a peer to the Azure deployment above, not a fallback or a secondary copy of it.
Everything Azure-specific above has an AWS counterpart behind the same app seams
(ADR 0010/0013/0028) — no app code differs between the clouds.

- **Infra runbook:** [`deploy/terraform/aws/README.md`](terraform/aws/README.md) —
  the OpenTofu stack (ECS Fargate api/worker/frontend + migrate task, RDS,
  ElastiCache, Cognito, Secrets Manager, CloudFront→ALB ingress, SES alerts, ADOT
  sidecars → X-Ray), the apply recipe, the state-encryption rules, and the
  `-replace` procedure for rolling task-definition changes.
- **Deploy workflow:** [`deploy-aws.yml`](../.github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml)
  (`workflow_dispatch`) — build → GHCR (`aws-<sha>` tags) → migrate RunTask gated
  on exit 0 → ECS rolls verified against the primary deployment's image → optional
  CloudFront smoke.

The AWS-shaped values for the production-prerequisites table above (all set by the
Terraform, listed here so the table's Azure values aren't mistaken for the only shape):

| Setting | AWS value |
|---|---|
| `SECRET_STORE` | `aws_secrets_manager` + `AWS_SECRETS_MANAGER_PREFIX` (default `dataq/`) — reads/writes Secrets Manager under the prefix via the **ECS task role**; no stored credential. Datasource credentials land as `<prefix>/conn-<type>-<qualifier>-<env>-<shortid>`, same naming convention as Key Vault. |
| OIDC (backend) | `OIDC_ISSUER` = the Cognito pool issuer, `OIDC_AUDIENCE` = the SPA client id — the provider-neutral `OidcBearerScheme` (ADR 0026 amendment); Cognito access tokens carry no `email`, resolved via the userinfo endpoint (#1346). |
| OIDC access gate | `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` (#1386) — who may hold a DataQ account on the generic-OIDC path. Empty = **no app-side gate**: every identity the issuer will mint a token for is auto-provisioned, so the IdP's registration policy becomes DataQ's. That state is logged at WARNING (`auth_oidc_no_signup_allowlist`) on every boot. Checked on every request, so removing an address also revokes an existing account. Unlike the OTP allowlist it defaults to open, because a fail-closed default would lock an existing workspace out on a routine image bump — the primary gate is the IdP (`allow_admin_create_user_only` on the Cognito pool). |
| Frontend auth | `DATAQ_AUTH_SCOPE="openid email profile"` (#1347 — Cognito rejects `offline_access`) and `DATAQ_AUTH_LOGOUT_STYLE=cognito` (#1364 — Cognito's non-conformant `/logout`). |
| `REDIS_URL` | `rediss://…?ssl_cert_reqs=required` (ElastiCache TLS; the app also defaults the parameter when absent — #1363). |
| `RATE_LIMIT_XFF_TRUSTED_HOPS` | `3` (CloudFront → ALB → nginx each append to `X-Forwarded-For`). |
| Email alerts | SES via `alert_email` (sender) / `alert_email_to` (recipients) Terraform vars — sandbox identities need a one-time verification click each (#1368). |
| Observability | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4318` → ADOT sidecar → X-Ray traces + CloudWatch OTel logs (#1369); container logs in CloudWatch `/dataq-app/*`. |

Pass that password at apply time as `TF_VAR_app_db_password` (it becomes the
`DATABASE_URL` Container App secret; never committed). The app reaches the server
at runtime over the server's allow-Azure-services firewall rule.

## Apply

```bash
cd deploy/terraform/azure
tofu init
# image_tag / frontend_image_tag have no default: pass what prod runs NOW, so any
# app the apply creates (e.g. dataq-app-beat, #1811) starts on the live image.
IMG=$(az containerapp show -n dataq-app-worker -g dataq-rg --query 'properties.template.containers[0].image' -o tsv)
FE=$(az containerapp show -n dataq-app-frontend -g dataq-rg --query 'properties.template.containers[0].image' -o tsv)
TF_VAR_app_db_password='REDACTED' tofu plan -out=azure.plan \
  -var="image_tag=${IMG##*:}" -var="frontend_image_tag=${FE##*:}"   # review
tofu apply azure.plan
```

## After apply — wire the Deploy workflow

`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` reads these. Push them with `gh` from the outputs:

```bash

## Apply

```bash
cd deploy/terraform/aws
tofu init
# state_encryption_passphrase comes from your terraform.tfvars — see
# terraform.tfvars.example.
#
# Image tags (#1349): the services RUN these images from the first apply.
# publish-images.yml tags main merges as `main-<full sha>` (the bare `<sha>`
# tag is owned by the manual Azure deploy.yml and usually does NOT exist), and
# its `paths` filter skips merges that don't change image content — so use the
# last IMAGE-BEARING main commit, not the branch tip, and verify the tag
# exists before applying:
IMG_SHA=$(git log origin/main -1 --format=%H -- backend frontend pyproject.toml)
docker manifest inspect "ghcr.io/theurgicduke771/dataq-backend:main-${IMG_SHA}" > /dev/null  # must succeed
TF_VAR_app_db_password="REDACTED" \
tofu plan -input=false -out=tfplan \
  -var="image_tag=main-${IMG_SHA}" \
  -var="frontend_image_tag=main-${IMG_SHA}"
tofu apply -input=false tfplan
```

**Cost starts here.** `tofu apply` creates real, billable AWS resources (Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, ALB). Review the plan before applying. See the root-level deployment plan (in the session that built this stack) for the cost breakdown against the AWS free-tier credit.

> **Existing stack picking up a new service (e.g. `beat`, #1811)?** `tofu apply` first — the
> Deploy workflow only rolls images onto services that already exist, it never creates them.
> Applying registers `aws_ecs_service.beat` (family `dataq-app-beat`, fixed name, no new repo
> variable needed — `deploy-aws.yml` references it the same way it references the other three)
> **before** the next `deploy-aws.yml` dispatch tries to `update-service` it.

Both plans are ready. Nothing has been applied or deployed yet.

**Azure:** no infrastructure drift; the only change is one output value. No `tofu apply` is needed, only the Deploy workflow.

**AWS:** the plan is 4 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy.
- It creates the separate Celery `beat` service (task definition, log group and service). AWS has never had it; Azure got it on 09-27.
- It replaces the worker's task definition to drop `-B`, the embedded beat. The live AWS worker still runs `-B`. A plain apply would leave it there and start a second scheduler. Worse, `ecs_roll.sh` copies the latest worker revision into every future deploy, so the `-B` would never go away. The "destroy" is the old worker revision being deregistered; its running tasks keep running until the worker is updated.
- It updates the GitHub deploy role's policy to cover the new `beat` service.
- The DB password is carried over from the existing secret, so the database itself isn't touched.

| Step | Cloud | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | AWS | `tofu apply tfplan` (images stay on the current `aws-7a3244a4`) |
| 2 | AWS | Immediately point the worker service at its new revision without `-B`, so two schedulers overlap for only a minute or two. The job that dispatches scheduled runs locks each schedule row, so a duplicate tick can't dispatch a run twice. |
| 3 | AWS | Dispatch `deploy-aws.yml` on `9f5475b7`: 16 migrations, then roll api, worker, beat and frontend |
| 4 | Azure | Dispatch `deploy.yml` on `9f5475b7`: 6 migrations, then roll all four apps |

- **Databricks:** the ops log says the QA token must be rotated before today (09-30). The Unity Catalog checks may need a new token from you.
- **Snowflake:** its PATs expire on 10-11, so they're fine for this.

"""Post-deploy smoke + authenticated probes. FE and PAT come from the environment."""

import json
import os
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

FE = os.environ["FE"].rstrip("/")
PAT = os.environ.get("PAT", "")
EXPECT_TOOLS = int(os.environ.get("EXPECT_TOOLS", "52"))
fails: list[str] = []


def req(method, path, *, auth=False, body=None, headers=None, raw_url=None):
    h = dict(headers or {})
    if auth:
        h["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {PAT}"
    data = None
    if body is not None:
        data = json.dumps(body).encode()
        h.setdefault("Content-Type", "application/json")
    r = urllib.request.Request(raw_url or FE + path, data=data, method=method, headers=h)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(r, timeout=60) as resp:
            return resp.status, dict(resp.headers), resp.read()
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, dict(e.headers), e.read()


def check(label, cond, detail=""):
    print(f"{'PASS' if cond else 'FAIL'}  {label}  {detail}")
    if not cond:
        fails.append(label)


s, h, b = req("GET", "/healthz")
check("healthz 200", s == 200, s)
s, h, b = req("GET", "/")
check("SPA root 200", s == 200, s)
sec = [k for k in h if k.lower() in {
    "content-security-policy", "strict-transport-security", "x-content-type-options",
    "referrer-policy", "permissions-policy", "x-frame-options"}]
check("security headers 6/6", len(sec) == 6, sorted(k.lower() for k in sec))
check("no server version leak", "/" not in h.get("Server", h.get("server", "")), h.get("Server", ""))
s, _, _ = req("GET", "/suites")
check("deep link 200", s == 200, s)
s, _, _ = req("GET", "/api/v1/me")
check("api unauth 401", s == 401, s)
s, _, _ = req("GET", "/mcp/")
check("mcp GET unauth 401", s == 401, s)
s, _, _ = req("POST", "/mcp/", body={})
check("mcp POST unauth 401", s == 401, s)
s, _, _ = req("GET", "/api/v1/openapi.json")
check("openapi gated 404", s == 404, s)
s, _, b = req("GET", "/docs")
check("/docs is SPA shell", s == 200 and b"swagger" not in b.lower(), s)

if PAT:
    s, _, b = req("GET", "/api/v1/me", auth=True)
    me = json.loads(b) if s == 200 else {}
    check("me 200 (PAT)", s == 200, f"role={me.get('role')} admin={me.get('is_workspace_admin')}")
    name = me.get("display_name")
    if name:
        s, _, _ = req("PATCH", "/api/v1/me", auth=True, body={"display_name": name})
        check("PATCH /me 200 (write probe)", s == 200, s)
    s, _, b = req("GET", "/api/v1/connections", auth=True)
    conns = json.loads(b) if s == 200 else []
    items = conns.get("items", conns) if isinstance(conns, dict) else conns
    check("connections 200", s == 200, f"{len(items)} connections")
    for c in items:
        print(f"      conn {c.get('id')} {c.get('type'):<14} {c.get('name')}")
    mh = {"Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream"}
    s, rh, b = req("POST", "/mcp/", auth=True, headers=mh, body={
        "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize",
        "params": {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": {},
                   "clientInfo": {"name": "smoke", "version": "1"}}})
    sid = rh.get("mcp-session-id") or rh.get("Mcp-Session-Id")
    check("mcp initialize 200", s == 200 and bool(sid), s)
    if sid:
        mh["mcp-session-id"] = sid
        req("POST", "/mcp/", auth=True, headers=mh,
            body={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"})
        s, _, b = req("POST", "/mcp/", auth=True, headers=mh,
                      body={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/list"})
        text = b.decode()
        payload = text.split("data:", 1)[1] if "data:" in text else text
        tools = json.loads(payload).get("result", {}).get("tools", [])
        check(f"mcp tools/list = {EXPECT_TOOLS}", len(tools) == EXPECT_TOOLS, len(tools))

print(f"\n{len(fails)} failure(s): {fails}")
sys.exit(1 if fails else 0)
